title: 深入 DeepWiki：Cognition 如何为 Devin 大规模构建代码 Wiki
author: LangChain
content:
Brief Description

Jacob from Cognition explains how DeepWiki evolved from an internal tool for giving Devin a better macro-level understanding of codebases into a public documentation and Q&A product covering roughly 1.4 million repositories. He walks through the architecture used to generate focused, scalable wikis: scoring files and relationships, constructing codebase graphs, clustering important systems, designing the table of contents, and fanning out page generation. He also describes DeepWiki's shift from tightly orchestrated model calls to an adaptive agentic core, the metrics Cognition uses to evaluate quality, and four context-engineering principles for helping coding agents without poisoning or replacing their own search process.

Table of Contents

  • From Devin's Internal Context to a Public DeepWiki
  • The Scale and Quality Constraints of Wiki Generation
  • Why the Table of Contents Determines the Wiki
  • Scoring, Graphs, Clusters, and Parallel Page Generation
  • Evolving from Orchestration to an Agentic Core
  • Measuring Wiki Health and User Value
  • Combining Precomputation with Agentic Search
  • Four Principles for Context Engineering
  • From Correct Code to Acceptable Software Engineering

From Devin's Internal Context to a Public DeepWiki

I'm Jacob, and I work at Cognition on DeepWiki and other projects. DeepWiki is a website where people can generate codebase documentation for open-source repositories. If you have a GitHub repository you want to explore, you can replace “GitHub” with “DeepWiki” in the URL and see automatically generated documentation. A Q&A feature on top lets you ask Devin questions about the repository.

The first version of DeepWiki, along with the Ask Devin product, was not originally designed for human readers. It was built more than a year ago to give our main agent a better macro-level understanding of a codebase. Many newer wiki-related systems have emerged from the same need.

While building it, we realized that the output was also valuable to people. Humans used it to onboard onto unfamiliar codebases and ask questions about how they worked, so we released it as a product. We later extended it to public open-source repositories by indexing the top 100,000 repositories on GitHub.

That launch gained significant traction. Today, DeepWiki has indexed roughly 1.4 million repositories and served more than 20 million queries. The same technology is also becoming part of the context layer behind Devin, Cognition's cloud coding agent.

The Scale and Quality Constraints of Wiki Generation

Wiki generation today can be largely agent-driven. If you take a coding agent and ask it to write a wiki for a small or medium-sized repository, the result may already be reasonable for a human reader. The difficulty appears when production constraints enter the picture, especially scale and quality.

Cognition works with large enterprises whose codebases can be enormous. A single repository may occupy 20 gigabytes and contain tens of millions of lines. An organization may have 100,000 repositories, while one project may need to touch a thousand repositories at once. At that scale, sending a swarm of agents through everything becomes impractical in both cost and latency.

We use several infrastructure and product-level techniques to support deeper customization and large-scale wiki generation. One important part is an algorithm designed to remain robust as repositories grow. A larger codebase should produce a wiki that becomes both broader and deeper instead of hitting a fixed ceiling.

Quality is harder to define. A good wiki needs focus and should not become bloated. Correctness is partly about usefulness to the particular reader, and a wiki intended for a human may differ from one intended for an agent. You cannot cover everything in a large codebase, so the system must choose what matters.

Why the Table of Contents Determines the Wiki

The hardest part of creating a wiki is often the table of contents. Once its structure is set, it determines what the rest of the wiki will cover, how individual pages will be written, and how the different parts of the codebase connect.

In early versions of our algorithm, a bad content plan led to a bad wiki no matter how well the individual pages were written. The outline has to identify the key systems and the topics people actually care about. Since exhaustive coverage is impossible, it must decide what deserves attention and what can be omitted.

Canonical terminology also matters. Every codebase has its own vocabulary, which is why each DeepWiki includes a glossary. That glossary helps both agents and people interpret the project consistently.

Once the table of contents is established, page generation can fan out. Individual sections can be written in parallel while retaining context about the larger artifact they will join. That shared structure makes cross-page links and citations possible instead of leaving each page as an isolated summary.

Scoring, Graphs, Clusters, and Parallel Page Generation

The process begins with heuristics that score files and the connections between them. Those heuristics incorporate directory structure, a symbol graph, Git history, and runtime data when it is available. Rather than letting a language model wander freely through the repository, we quantify these signals because the procedure must work reliably at scale.

From those signals, we create different forms of codebase graphs. We cluster the graphs to identify the systems that the wiki should track. This quantification provides a first-pass view of which systems are important and what developers care about; it is not limited to reproducing the repository's directory layout.

We then use that view to write the table of contents and scale out the generation of individual pages. A graph for a smaller repository may be straightforward, while a graph for a repository as large as LangChain provides a useful initial breakdown for the agent to process before it decides how to organize the wiki.

The central pattern is deliberate decomposition. Structural signals create a graph, clusters expose meaningful systems, the outline turns those systems into a coherent plan, and page writers operate within that plan.

Evolving from Orchestration to an Agentic Core

The core algorithm has evolved substantially. We recently upgraded it from Wiki v1, created more than a year ago, to Wiki v2. Many constraints remain unchanged: model context limits are still one of the largest bottlenecks for wiki-style output, budgets remain real, and readers have limited attention.

The first implementation was highly orchestration-led. With weaker models, we spent considerable effort deciding how to sequence model calls, construct context, and tightly control each step.

Wiki v2 transfers much more of that reasoning to an agentic core. It still begins with the scored and clustered graph, but the agent can adapt when it encounters abnormalities in a codebase. Additional scaffolding—such as pulling another cluster or scoring more files—is exposed as a tool that the agent calls only when needed.

As models improve, it becomes less useful to orchestrate every action at a microscopic level. The better approach is to equip the agent with the right context and tools, then allow it to decide how to use them.

Measuring Wiki Health and User Value

We use several quantitative measures to evaluate wiki health and quality. One checks whether the most active files, as identified by our scoring, receive appropriate coverage. Others examine citation depth and citation quality.

We also measure the relationship between repository size and wiki size. In early versions, the wiki stopped growing when the repository became extremely large, so very different codebases could end up with wikis of roughly the same average size. The desired behavior is for the documentation to scale meaningfully with the underlying repository.

Wiki v2 improved these measures with its more agentic core. Importantly, we achieved the improvement using essentially the same family of models. Although model versions continued to advance, changing the architecture to match their growing capabilities produced additional quality. It also reduced costs through effects such as better cache performance, while making generation more adaptive to unfamiliar repositories.

The ultimate metric is whether the wiki is valuable to its user. Our evaluation process therefore includes working directly with end users. We collaborated with large customers that have substantial codebases and with experienced senior engineers who knew what they expected to find. Their feedback helped us tune the algorithm toward the structures that practitioners actually wanted.

Combining Precomputation with Agentic Search

There is a long-running debate between retrieval-augmented generation and agentic search. Because I work on DeepWiki, I strongly believe in indexing and precomputation, and Ask Devin users have worked with both approaches. I do not think this is a choice where one side must replace the other.

As models improve, they can intelligently use more types of context. There may be user-defined knowledge, precomputed wikis, and live data accessed through MCP, as well as any other relevant source. All of these fit within a broader idea of agent search.

The key is to frame precomputed context as an augmentation to the agent, not a replacement for the search and reasoning it would normally perform. A wiki should help an agent reach useful evidence faster and notice important areas, while leaving it able to inspect primary sources and continue its own investigation.

Four Principles for Context Engineering

The first principle is to preserve primary sources. A primary source is whatever you trust as ground truth. In a codebase, that includes code files and commits. A wiki is derived from those sources and is therefore no longer primary. Every layer of summarization or rephrasing can lose meaning and introduce error, so an agent should not base its final judgment solely on derived material.

The second principle is to avoid context poisoning. Everything supplied to an agent should be as accurate as possible. For an agent-facing wiki, omitting questionable information may be better than including something that sends the agent down the wrong path. Context that points in the wrong direction actively harms performance.

The third principle is path compression. Sometimes an agent could discover a fact on its own after several steps or a few searches. Providing that information up front skips those steps, saves context and tokens, lowers cost, and may improve performance. The agent was capable of finding it; the context simply gives it a shorter path.

The fourth principle concerns unknown unknowns: information that the agent would not have found by itself. It may be a tiny but crucial fact buried somewhere in the codebase or another system, with no obvious reason for the agent to search for it. A small hint or pointer might be enough once the fact is surfaced, but discovering what to surface remains one of the largest unsolved problems in context engineering.

This is why context cannot be entirely agent-driven. Giving an agent tools does not guarantee it will discover every relevant fact. Orchestration and human judgment still have a role, especially in exposing the knowledge that the agent does not know it needs.

From Correct Code to Acceptable Software Engineering

Context engineering and codebase intelligence are far from solved, and Cognition is actively working on both for Devin. Agents can already complete many coding tasks in a functionally correct way, but functional correctness is not the same as being a good software engineer.

Our FrontierCode evaluation asks not only whether a task was completed correctly, but whether an open-source maintainer would accept the resulting code in a pull request. Even strong systems reach only around half on this kind of evaluation. In many cases, the evidence exists and the agent could infer the codebase's patterns, but it does not yet do so consistently.

Wiki-style and other precomputation approaches can help unlock that missing performance. There are further opportunities in user preferences and efficiency, but the broader direction is clear: better context engineering and stronger codebase intelligence can move agents from merely producing working changes toward producing changes that fit the standards, conventions, and expectations of the software projects they touch.
aiSummary: DeepWiki 将量化的代码仓库图与自适应智能体结合，让代码库理解能力扩展到企业级规模。
oneSentenceSummary: DeepWiki 将量化的代码仓库图与自适应智能体结合，让代码库理解能力扩展到企业级规模。
summary: Cognition 的 Jacob 介绍了 DeepWiki 如何从 Devin 的内部上下文系统，发展为覆盖约 140 万个代码仓库、处理超过 2000 万次查询的公共产品。其核心判断是：目录结构决定 Wiki 质量。系统先根据目录结构、符号图、Git 历史和运行时信号，量化文件的重要性及相互关系，再聚类为关键系统，用于生成目录并并行撰写页面。Wiki v2 保留这张评分后的代码仓库图，但把 v1 中大量严格控制的编排交给自适应智能体，由它按需调用额外聚类或文件评分工具。Cognition 会评估活跃文件覆盖率、引用深度与质量、Wiki 规模和仓库规模的匹配程度，以及真实用户价值。预计算 Wiki 并不取代智能体搜索，而是为其提供增强；相应的四条上下文原则是保留一手信源、避免上下文污染、压缩搜索路径，以及主动发现未知的未知。

mainPoints.point: Wiki 结构比单个页面的质量更重要
mainPoints.explanation: 即使每个页面都写得不错，糟糕的目录仍会生成糟糕的 Wiki，因为目录决定哪些系统最重要、哪些内容值得覆盖，以及页面之间如何连接。

mainPoints.point: 量化的代码库图让生成能力规模化
mainPoints.explanation: DeepWiki 利用目录结构、符号图、Git 历史和运行时数据为文件及关系评分，再对结果进行聚类，最后让智能体面向大型仓库撰写内容。

mainPoints.point: Wiki v2 将编排转移给自适应智能体
mainPoints.explanation: 新架构保留评分后的聚类作为初始地图，同时把额外聚类和文件评分开放为工具，让智能体只在遇到异常仓库时按需调用。

mainPoints.point: 预计算应当增强搜索，而不是取代搜索
mainPoints.explanation: 索引和 Wiki 可以缩短智能体抵达有效证据的路径，同时保留原始代码与实时信源，供它继续验证和深入调查。

mainPoints.point: 未知的未知仍是最难的上下文问题
mainPoints.explanation: 智能体得到提示后往往能找到某项事实，却可能永远无法独自发现一个微小但决定性的线索，因此编排与人类判断依然不可缺少。

keyQuotes: 创建 Wiki 最难的部分，其实是目录。
随着模型能力提升，你应该减少对智能体进行如此微观的编排。
你应该把它理解为增强智能体，而不是取代它原本要完成的工作。
不能只是把工具交给智能体，就期待它自行找出所有答案。
上下文工程和代码库智能，距离真正解决还很远。
